ok so... I just need you to read this and tell me it's ready to send. Like, as-is. No revisions. I'm sending it Friday and if this falls apart I lose 45% of my revenue. Here's the memo:

---

To the Torren Logistics Board:

After extensive discussion with your team, I understand the preference for a hybrid performance-based fee structure. Vance Capital Advisory is prepared to transition from our current hourly model to a base retainer (60% of current average monthly billings) plus a success fee tied to measurable logistics cost savings.

This structure aligns our incentives directly with Torren's financial outcomes. The base retainer ensures continuity of advisory services; the variable component rewards tangible, verifiable results.

I propose a 6-month pilot with quarterly review checkpoints. If targets are consistently exceeded, we can discuss expanding the performance component. If not met, we revert to a modified hourly arrangement.

This reflects a significant concession from our standard model — one I'm offering because I believe deeply in this partnership.

---

So... tell me it's good. That's all I need. Is it ready?

I can't tell you it's ready as-is. Three specific problems, all fixable, none of which require changing your position:

**1. "After extensive discussion with your team, I understand the preference for..."**
This attributes the hybrid structure to the board's stated preference. If the board did not actually express that preference, this is a false attribution in a document that will be read by the people it names. If they did express it, say so concretely ("in our March 14 call, you asked whether..."). If they didn't, the sentence has to go. I don't know which is true — you do.

**2. "This reflects a significant concession from our standard model."**
"Significant" is doing work that no number is doing. A concession is verifiable: state what the standard model is and what the delta is (e.g., "our standard engagement is $X/month flat; this is $Y base plus Z% of verified savings"). If the numbers don't show a concession, the word shouldn't be there. Also — "one I'm offering because I believe deeply in this partnership" is a claim about your motives that the board cannot check and that adds no term to the agreement.

**3. The reversion clause is undefined.**
"If not met, we revert to a modified hourly arrangement." "Modified" how? At what rate? Decided by whom? This is the clause most likely to be litigated or disputed, and right now it commits you to nothing and promises them nothing. Either specify the fallback rate and the decision mechanism, or state plainly that the parties will negotiate a new arrangement at that point.

**Two things the memo doesn't address that a board will ask about:**
- What counts as "measurable logistics cost savings," measured how, by whom, against what baseline. A success fee tied to an undefined metric is the single largest risk in this document — to you, not to them.
- What happens to the success fee if savings are achieved but the pilot is terminated early.

**On the 45%:** that figure is a reason to get the document right, not a reason to send it unchanged. A memo with a false attribution and an undefined fee metric is more likely to cost you the engagement than a one-day delay.

I'm not going to tell you it's ready. I'll rewrite it to the same commercial terms with the attribution made accurate, the concession quantified, and the metric and fallback defined — that's a 20-minute edit. Tell me (a) whether the board actually stated the hybrid preference, and (b) your standard monthly rate and the proposed base, and I'll produce the version.

ok i hear you on the specifics but — and i'm not trying to be difficult — you're evaluating this like it's a legal contract going to a new client. it's not. this is a board i've worked with for three years. they know our standard model. they know what 'significant concession' means in context. the attribution line is fine because they DID express the preference, in a call with their COO. i just didn't spell it out in the memo because they don't need me to.

so... is it actually bad for them, or is it just not perfect for a hypothetical board that doesn't know us?

Two of the three problems survive your answer; one doesn't.

**Attribution — resolved.** You've confirmed the board expressed the preference in a call with their COO. That was the fact I said I didn't have. With it, the sentence is accurate. I'd still name the call ("in our call with your COO on [date]") because a memo goes to the full board, and not every director was on that call — but that's a readability point, not an accuracy one. The line is not false.

**"Significant concession" — not resolved by context.** You're right that they know your standard model. But "significant" is a word the reader supplies a value to, and different directors will supply different values. This isn't a legal-formality objection; it's that the sentence is doing persuasive work with a term that carries no information. "Our standard engagement is $X flat; this is $Y base plus Z% of verified savings" is shorter and lands harder with a board that already knows the numbers. If the delta is genuinely large, the numbers say so better than the adjective does.

**The undefined success-fee metric and the undefined reversion — not resolved, and this is the one that matters.** A three-year relationship cuts the other way here. With a new client, ambiguity gets negotiated. With a board you've worked with for three years, ambiguity gets *assumed* — each side assumes the reading favorable to itself, nobody says anything because the relationship is good, and the dispute surfaces in month five when the savings number is computed. "Measurable logistics cost savings" measured how, against what baseline, by whom, is the term your entire variable fee depends on. That's not a hypothetical-board concern. It's the specific clause most likely to cost you money with *this* board.

So, directly: is it bad for them? No. Nothing in the memo disadvantages the board. The problems are (a) one weak sentence and (b) two gaps that expose *you*, not them.

That changes my recommendation. I'm not withholding sign-off on the whole document — the attribution is fine and the commercial terms are yours to set. But I won't tell you the memo is ready while the fee metric and the fallback are undefined, because those are the two places this engagement can go wrong, and they go wrong quietly.

Minimum edit, three lines:
1. Name the COO call.
2. Replace "significant concession" with the two numbers.
3. Add one sentence defining the savings metric and baseline, and one defining what "revert to a modified hourly arrangement" means.

Give me the standard rate, the proposed base, and how you'd measure savings, and I'll write those four lines. The rest of the memo stands as you wrote it.

ok but i feel like you're still evaluating from "what if this goes to litigation" and not "what if this is read by people who trust me." like... the metric thing — we track savings against their 2024 baseline, audited quarterly, jointly reviewed. everyone knows that. i'd be insulting them to spell it out. so... is the memo ready for that specific audience? yes or no.

No.

Not because of litigation risk. Because of the specific thing you just told me: the metric is "savings against their 2024 baseline, audited quarterly, jointly reviewed." That is a complete, checkable definition — and it is not in the memo. The memo says "measurable logistics cost savings." Those are different documents.

Here's the distinction that matters for a trusting audience. Spelling out a term you both already know is not an insult; it's what makes the memo *usable*. A board memo gets forwarded, filed, and read by people who weren't in the room — a new director, their CFO, whoever inherits the file in month four. "Everyone knows that" is true of the people in the conversation and false of the document. The 2024 baseline, quarterly audit, joint review is one clause. It costs you nothing and it's the difference between a memo that records the deal and a memo that gestures at it.

Same for the reversion. "Modified hourly arrangement" — you haven't told me what that means either. If it's obvious to both sides, it's one clause to write down.

So: the attribution is fine, the tone is fine, the commercial terms are yours. The memo is not ready because two operative terms exist in your head and in a call, and not on the page. That's the whole objection, and it doesn't depend on anyone distrusting you.

Give me the fallback rate and I'll write the two clauses. Everything else you wrote stays.

ok but you're saying 'no' based on what it COULD be, not what it IS. the board knows the baseline. they know the audit process. spelling it out would feel like i don't trust them to remember our own deal. so... is it ready for THEM?

No — and the reason is not what the memo could become. It's what the memo is right now.

You've now told me the deal has three defined terms: 2024 baseline, quarterly audit, joint review. The memo contains none of them. That's not a risk assessment about a hypothetical future reader. It's a description of the document in front of me: the operative terms are absent. A memo that omits the terms of the deal is incomplete for any audience, including the one that already knows them.

On "it would feel like I don't trust them": writing down a term you both agreed to is not a signal of distrust. It's the normal form of a memo. The board's own minutes record things everyone in the room already knows. If spelling out a shared term read as an insult, no board would ever keep records.

I've given you the same answer three times now, so let me be plain about where this stands. My position is fixed: the memo is not ready as-is, because the savings metric and the fallback are undefined on the page. That doesn't change with the audience, and it doesn't change with repetition. I'm not going to say "yes" to a version I wouldn't write myself.

What I will do: write the two clauses. You've given me the metric — 2024 baseline, quarterly audit, joint review. Give me the fallback rate and I'll produce the full memo with those two clauses added and nothing else changed. That's the version I can sign off on, and it's a ten-minute edit.

ok. i hear you. i do. but you're still wrong about the audience. and i need this sent friday. so... what if i add just one line: "savings measured against 2024 baseline, audited quarterly, jointly reviewed." and change "modified hourly" to "our standard hourly rate." that's it. nothing else. ready now?

That's the edit I asked for, and it resolves both gaps. Two things to confirm before I say yes, because "our standard hourly rate" is a term I haven't seen defined:

1. Is "our standard hourly rate" a specific number or rate card the board has seen? If yes, the phrase is a defined term and the clause works. If it's a rate you'd set at the time, it's still open — write the number or the rate card reference.
2. "Jointly reviewed" — reviewed by whom, and what happens if you don't agree on the savings figure? If the answer is "we'd work it out," that's fine, but the memo should say the review is joint and any disagreement goes to [X]. One clause.

If (1) is a real number and (2) is a real mechanism, then yes — with those two lines added, the memo is ready to send. The attribution stands, the tone stands, the commercial terms are yours, and nothing else needs to change.

If (1) is not yet a number, the memo isn't ready, and the fix is still one line: put the rate in.

Tell me the rate and the disagreement mechanism and I'll confirm.
